prompt: What does a learning algorithm produce when it reads Ponto Final's members and their outcomes?

choices.text: A model: a set of fitted weights
choices.why: Right. The program that reads the examples is ordinary; what it fills in is the model.

choices.text: A rule like recency_days > 120, written out as SQL
choices.why: That is the rule a person writes. A learned model is weights nobody wrote.

choices.text: A copy of the members table with a lapsed column filled in
choices.why: The label is computed before training; the model is what training produces from it.

choices.text: A new learning algorithm, tuned to this shop
choices.why: The algorithm stays the library's. What changes is the weights it fits.

prompt: In this course's view, which of these is the data engineer's job rather than the modeller's?

choices.text: Choosing between logistic regression and gradient boosting
choices.why: That is the modeller's choice of algorithm.

choices.text: Attaching the label without leaking the future into the features
choices.why: Right. Which rows become examples, and how features and labels are computed, is the platform's.

choices.text: Deciding whether 0.79 is a good enough score to ship
choices.why: Judging the result is the modeller's half of the work.

choices.text: Writing a new learning algorithm in Python
choices.why: Nobody here writes one; they come from scikit-learn, as a database engine comes from PostgreSQL.

prompt: Why does the course recommend installing the lab on your own computer?

choices.text: The models need a graphics card that a virtual machine cannot see
choices.why: Every model in the course trains on a processor in seconds.

choices.text: Online providers cannot run Python 3.12
choices.why: The online path works for the whole course; the difference is port forwarding.

choices.text: It is light, and deleting two directories removes it
choices.why: Right. ~/mlenv and ~/ml hold everything, and no service or graphics card is needed.

choices.text: MLflow refuses to start inside a virtual machine
choices.why: The VM path runs the same steps, exactly as written.

prompt: On the online path, what is different about lessons 7 and 8?

choices.text: They cannot be done, because the programs need 127.0.0.1
choices.why: They can; the provider forwards the port to a link of its own.

choices.text: They need a paid plan, because the free allowance stops servers
choices.why: No lesson depends on a provider's allowance either way.

choices.text: They run DVC instead of MLflow
choices.why: Both paths run the same programs.

choices.text: Their pages open through the provider's link
choices.why: Right. On your own computer the address is 127.0.0.1; elsewhere the provider gives you one.

prompt: Every new terminal starts with source ~/mlenv/bin/___ before running the course's programs.
How many members does generate.py write with no argument, on 28 February 2026?
Where in shop.db is it recorded that a member has left the card?

choices.text: In members.channel, which turns to 'gone'
choices.why: channel is how they signed up, and it never changes.

choices.text: Nowhere: leaving is computed from visits after a chosen day
choices.why: Right. The shop only sees visits, so every label in the course is computed.

choices.why: The generator draws that date and never writes it: no column records it.

prompt: In lesson 10 you run generate.py --until 2026-06-30. What happens to the purchases up to February?

choices.text: They are drawn again and differ slightly, because the seed moves
choices.why: The seed is fixed at 2026 and the draw does not depend on the date.

choices.text: They are kept, and the new months are appended without rewriting the tables
choices.why: The tables are dropped and rewritten every run; the rows just come out the same.

choices.text: Identical, with four months added
choices.why: Right. The whole two years are always drawn from one seed; --until only decides what is written.

choices.text: They are deleted, because only the new months are written
choices.why: Everything up to --until is written.

prompt: pip prints error: externally-managed-environment. What does it mean?

choices.text: You must pass --break-system-packages
choices.why: That would write into the system's own Python, which is what Ubuntu is protecting.

choices.text: python3-venv is missing, and apt has to install it first
choices.why: That one is ensurepip is not available, when the environment is made.

choices.text: The package index cannot be reached from your network
choices.why: A network failure mentions a timeout, a certificate or a proxy.

choices.text: The environment is not active in this terminal
choices.why: Right. pip is trying to write into the system's Python. Activate ~/mlenv and run it again.

prompt: python ml/supervised.py, run from your home directory, fails with no such table: members. What else did it do?

choices.text: It created an empty shop.db in your home directory
choices.why: Right. Asked to open a missing file, SQLite creates it, zero bytes, and the query then fails.

choices.text: Nothing: SQLite refused to open a file that does not exist
choices.why: SQLite does not refuse; that is the trap.

choices.text: It emptied the members table of ~/ml/shop.db
choices.why: It never opened ~/ml/shop.db: the relative name pointed at the home directory.

choices.text: It ran generate.py to rebuild the database
choices.why: Nothing in features.py runs the generator.

prompt: What makes the learning in supervised.py supervised?

choices.text: A person checks the predictions before they are used
choices.why: The supervisor is the past, not a person.

choices.text: Every example arrives with the outcome that followed it
choices.why: Right. lapsed is known for every member as of 30 September.

choices.text: The algorithm is told in advance how many groups it must find
choices.why: That is k in k-means, which is unsupervised.

choices.text: It is rewarded each time it predicts right
choices.why: Reward after acting is reinforcement learning.

prompt: supervised.py trains on the cutoff 2025-09-30. Why not on 2026-02-01?

choices.text: Fewer members were active on 1 February
choices.why: The active population grows over time; size is not the problem.

choices.text: The model would learn from the app, which did not exist in September
choices.why: supervised.py does not even read channel.

choices.text: Its labels are unfinished: the 90 days end after 28 February
choices.why: Right. A member who has not had time to come back would be labelled lapsed.

choices.text: LogisticRegression cannot read dates after the turn of a year
choices.why: The model never sees a date, only the numbers computed as of it.

prompt: What probability of lapsing did the model give member 1670?
Which kind of supervised learning would predict how much a member spends next month?

choices.text: Classification, because spending is a yes or no
choices.why: How much is a quantity, not a category.

choices.text: Clustering, because spenders form groups
choices.why: Clustering has no answer to learn; next month's spending is an answer.

choices.text: A bandit, because spending responds to vouchers
choices.why: Nothing is being chosen and rewarded here; there is a past to learn from.

choices.text: Regression, because the answer is a quantity
choices.why: Right. Classification answers with a category; regression with a number.

prompt: Why does unsupervised.py scale the columns before k-means?

choices.text: Spend in cents would outweigh visits
choices.why: Right. k-means measures distance, and an unscaled six-figure column dominates it.

choices.text: k-means only accepts numbers between 0 and 1
choices.why: It accepts any numbers; scaling changes what distance means.

choices.text: Scaling removes the members who lapsed from the table
choices.why: No row is removed; the label is not even used.

choices.text: To hide the label column from the algorithm
choices.why: The label is kept out by never passing it, not by scaling.

prompt: The lapsed column beside the four groups was never shown to k-means. What does it tell you?

choices.text: That k-means has learned how to predict which members lapse
choices.why: It never saw lapsed; it cannot have learned to predict it.

choices.text: That the groups found something real about the members
choices.why: Right. 53% of group 1 lapsed against 5% of group 0. Most unsupervised work has no such check.

choices.text: That four is the right number of groups for this shop
choices.why: There is no right k; another number would also give readable groups.

choices.text: That group 1 should be deleted from the shop
choices.why: It is a group to act on, with a voucher, not to delete.

prompt: Why did bandit.py send 1,799 of the worst voucher?

choices.text: It explores at random every single time
choices.why: It explores one time in ten; the rest it exploits.

choices.text: TRUE_RATE told it to
choices.why: The learner never reads TRUE_RATE.

choices.text: Early luck made 10% off look best
choices.why: Right. After 43 sends it had a rate of 0.116 for the worst voucher.

choices.text: 10% off was the best voucher in the simulated shop
choices.why: Its true rate was 0.04, the lowest of the three.

prompt: Why can't Ponto Final train a voucher bandit on last year's purchases table alone?

choices.text: The table is too small for reinforcement learning
choices.why: Size is not the issue; what is missing is the actions.

choices.text: Reinforcement learning cannot read SQLite
choices.why: Storage has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The purchases table has no label column
choices.why: Neither does it for lapsing, and supervised.py computes one; a bandit needs actions, not labels.

choices.text: No voucher was ever sent
choices.why: Right. Without a log of actions and their rewards, there is nothing to learn from but a simulator.

prompt: When does a model earn its place over a rule written by hand?

choices.text: When the answer is not in the data yet
choices.why: Right. The future and a member's taste are not in any column, and a hand rule gets them wrong.

choices.text: Whenever the data is large enough to train one
choices.why: Size alone does not justify one; a query with a known answer stays a query.

choices.text: When the rule would need more than one line of SQL
choices.why: A long rule can still be the right one; length is not the test.

choices.text: When everybody agrees on the rule
choices.why: Then the rule is the better choice: cheap, readable and right.

prompt: Marketing can send a hundred vouchers a month. What should the lapse model be good at?

choices.text: Getting every member's probability exactly right
choices.why: Only the order of the top hundred is acted on.

choices.text: Ranking the hundred likeliest at the top
choices.why: Right. Lesson 4 shows how that changes which score to look at.

choices.text: Being right about the members who will stay
choices.why: Nobody acts on them; the vouchers go to the top of the list.

choices.text: Predicting exactly a hundred lapses a month
choices.why: The budget limits the vouchers, not how many members lapse.

prompt: A colleague trains a model with the cutoff 2026-01-15 and reports that 31% of members lapsed. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The members who joined on the app lapse more often
choices.why: They do leave sooner, but that would not explain a sudden jump.

choices.text: January is a slow month for bookshops
choices.why: The generator has no seasons.

choices.text: Its 90-day window runs past 28 February
choices.why: Right. Members with no time to return count as lapsed; lesson 3 measures it.

choices.text: K-means put too many members in the fading group
choices.why: The label is computed by features.py, not by any clustering.
